# Trip Packing List

## Overview

One 40 litre bag is all I take now, cabin size on every airline I use, with a 7 kg target on the scale at home before I leave. The bag opens flat like a suitcase, which makes the packing cubes work, and it has two compression straps and a small top pocket I keep empty until security. I check it on a kitchen scale the night before, because the limit bites on the cheap tickets, and I have never once paid for a checked bag since I started travelling this way. The rule is simple: everything goes in the one bag, and the spare set of everything small lives inside it rather than in a separate pouch.

Three packing cubes do the organising: one for tops, one for trousers and shorts, and one for the small things. Three days of clothes is the number I pack, washed as I go, which covers a week or more with a sink, a line and a little soap. The bag weighs about 6.5 kg when I set off, and a week in it weighs the same, because the washing keeps the pile flat. I would rather do laundry in an evening than carry a heavier bag up four flights of stairs.

## Notes

The cubes are the trick. Rolled, not folded, and packed tight, three days of clothes compress into a third of the bag and leave room for the cables pouch, a book and the wash bag. I wash every second or third evening, a sink of cool water and a few drops of soap, wring in a towel and hang on a line I string across the room. By morning everything is dry, or dry enough to finish on the back of a chair. In warm places I wash more often and carry less; in cold places I add a base layer and accept a heavier bag.

The cables pouch holds two chargers, a short cable of each kind, a power bank, a plug adapter and a small headphone case, and it never leaves the bag. It is the one item I check twice before leaving the room, because a misplaced cable is the thing that ruins an evening. The spare set is small: a second pair of socks, a second phone cable, a spare pair of glasses and a spare bank card kept apart from the wallet. None of it weighs much and all of it has saved a day at some point.

The security tray routine is the same every time: jacket off and folded into the tray first, then the bag, then the pouch on top where I can see it come through, then the phone and the belt. Liquids stay in the wash bag in the easy-to-reach pocket until the last moment. I hold the passport in my hand, not in the tray. I stopped carrying a laptop on short trips, and I stopped carrying the third pair of shoes, the paper guidebook, the umbrella I never used and the full-size toiletry bottles that always leaked. Everything I took out has stayed out, and the bag has gone with me everywhere since.

## Troubleshooting

When the bag will not close, take out the heaviest item and wear it through the airport, which is nearly always the jacket. If the airline weighs the bag at the gate, the jacket goes on and the bag is suddenly under the limit.

If a zipper sticks, rub the teeth with a candle stub from the hotel or a little soap, and it will run smoothly for the rest of the trip. A cube that is too full will not compress, so leave the top third of each one empty and roll tighter.

When the wash does not dry overnight, hang it on the shower rail with the bathroom door open rather than over a chair, and wring it once more in a towel. Damp clothes on the last morning go into a plastic bag and straight into the wash at home.

If the cables pouch goes missing, the spare phone cable and the spare bank card cover the gap until it turns up, which is why the spares travel apart from the main pouch. A flat power bank is the one failure that has no fix, so I charge it every second night whether I have used it or not.

When the bag itself is damaged, the repair is a needle and dental floss, which I now carry in the pouch, and it has held a torn strap for a whole trip.
